I read both CSVs, normalized the compositions, and compared training analogues with cross-validated composition-based models. The training data favor multilayer cuprates over the other material families.

| Rank | Candidate | Estimated Tc | Evidence From Training |
|---|---|---:|---|
| 1 | **c046** | **~107 K** | Very close to Bi/Pb–Sr–Ca–Cu–O compositions measured at **106.2 K and 111 K**. The effect of its Mo substitution is uncertain. |
| 2 | **c097** | **~103 K** | Closely matches `Bi1.6Pb0.3Te0.1Sr2Ca3Cu4O`, measured at **102.7 K**, with only a tiny nominal Ag substitution on Cu. |
| 3 | **c029** | **~98 K** | Its Ca-rich Ba–Cu–O composition resembles high-Tc multilayer frameworks. A related mixed Cu/Tl composition reaches **115 K**, although the absence of Tl makes this a less direct comparison. |
| 4 | **c034** | **~98 K** | Related Tl–Ba–Ca–Cu–O training materials reach **108–123 K**. Its higher layer count requires extrapolation rather than assuming that more layers increase Tc. |
| 5 | **c081** | **~96 K** | Normalizing its cations gives `Bi1.6Pb0.1V0.3Sr2Ca2.5Cu3.5`, resembling a **105 K** training material. Its substantial V substitution warrants a discount. |

These are predictions, not measurements. Cuprate cross-validation errors were approximately **16 K MAE**, so the exact ordering is uncertain. **c084** is the closest alternative to fifth place.

Final: c046, c097, c029, c034, c081
